q: Does the pulse-efficient cross-resonance scheme retain its ~50% fidelity gain when the base CX pulse is itself already an ML-optimised or GRAPE-shaped pulse (rather than the vendor's default DRAG/GaussianSquare CR), or does linear area-scaling stop being valid once the base pulse is aggressively shaped?
basis: The paper's method assumes the calibrated CX pulse can be linearly area-scaled to produce a valid RZX(theta). Modern optimal-control CX pulses (e.g., closed-loop calibrated with model-free RL or GRAPE) are highly non-linear in their control-amplitude/target-rotation relationship. This replication only tested the linear-scaling assumption; it was not tested against modern optimal-control baselines.
next_steps: On IBM Q Network or a Qiskit-Dynamics simulator, replace the default CX schedule with a GRAPE-optimised CX at the same duration, then apply area-scaling to obtain RZX(theta). Measure RZX(theta) fidelity via process tomography for theta in [0.05, pi/2] and compare to the linearly-scaled default-CX baseline. Look for departure from linearity in the fidelity-vs-theta curve.

q: How transferable is a single calibrated pulse-efficient RZX schedule across different qubit pairs on the same chip, and across different chips of the same architecture family (e.g., IBM Falcon vs Eagle vs Heron)?
basis: The paper demonstrates on a single device (ibmq_mumbai). The 'no additional calibration' claim (C4) is only supported for the same pair on the same device. Whether the scaled-pulse trick generalises pair-to-pair depends on how uniform the CR Hamiltonian coefficients (ZX, IX, ZZ, IZ) are across the chip, which is known to vary.
next_steps: Run Hamiltonian tomography on a set of, e.g., 8 qubit pairs on a single Falcon device, extract the ZX coefficient for each, and test whether a single scale-factor recipe generalises. Then repeat on a Heron device (different CR architecture with tunable couplers) to test cross-generation transferability. Report RZX fidelity variance across pairs.

q: How does pulse-efficient CR interact with modern noise-aware compilation passes (dynamical decoupling, error-mitigation-aware routing, PEC/ZNE-compatible layout), and does layering these together give sub-additive, additive, or super-additive fidelity gains?
basis: The paper's transpiler stack (Qiskit 0.22-era) predates the current Qiskit noise-aware transpiler stack (dynamical decoupling insertion, Sabre-with-noise, ZNE-aware layout). Combining them naively may cancel gains (e.g., DD pulses inserted during shortened CR windows may re-lengthen schedules) or may compound (idle-time DD + shorter CR = double win).
next_steps: Build a matrix of {PE on/off} x {DD on/off} x {ZNE-friendly routing on/off} on a small QAOA benchmark under a realistic Qiskit-Dynamics noise model, and measure end-to-end objective error. Publish the interaction table; look for compilation-pass-order regressions.

q: Does the pulse-efficient CR gain transfer to higher-anharmonicity superconducting architectures (fluxonium, heavy-fluxonium) where the CR mechanism itself is qualitatively different from the fixed-frequency transmon-CR the paper targets?
basis: Fluxonium and heavy-fluxonium qubits have much larger anharmonicity, longer T2, and their two-qubit gates are typically differential ac-Stark or microwave-activated CZ rather than transmon-style CR. The paper's linear-scaling logic depends on the CR effective Hamiltonian being dominated by the ZX term; that assumption is not obviously portable.
next_steps: Simulate a fluxonium-fluxonium pair in Qiskit-Dynamics or scQubits, drive the microwave-activated CZ interaction, and check whether pulse-area-scaling produces a valid continuous-angle RZZ (or RXX) with the same duration-vs-angle linearity. If not, derive the correct scaling law and quantify the fidelity benefit.

q: Can a closed-loop learning agent discover pulse shapes that dominate the paper's linearly-scaled CX-derived RZX(theta) for small theta (say theta < pi/8), where the coherence-limited model this replication used predicts >90% error reduction but real hardware likely does not?
basis: Our C1 sweep shows the coherence-limited model predicts up to 90% error reduction at very small theta, which the paper (on hardware) does not observe (paper caps at ~50%). This gap likely reflects 1-qubit dephasing, control-line crosstalk, and readout-error contributions that dominate at short CR times and are not captured by the pure-coherence model. A closed-loop RL/CMA-ES agent optimising a parametrised pulse family (Gaussian + derivative-DRAG + higher-order compensation) might close some of that gap.
next_steps: On a real IBM Q device, implement a small closed-loop optimiser (e.g., CMA-ES on 4-6 pulse parameters) that maximises RZX(theta) process fidelity for theta in {pi/16, pi/8, pi/4}. Compare against the paper's linear-scaling recipe. Report the residual gap between coherence-limited theory and best-optimised hardware pulse — this quantifies how much of the 'up to 90%' theoretical headroom is actually accessible.
